expectations.text: Correctly identifies the code as internal/app-module (Tier 0) and scopes the review to rules that apply.
expectations.evidence: Dedicated section 'Tier classification (what I'm holding it to)': 'This is an `internal class` in an Android app's `ui.settings` package... Single target, single module, no `commonMain`, no `expect`/`actual`, no `publishing {}`... So this review is **Tier 0 (Core Kotlin) only**.' Findings header: 'Findings (Tier 0, highest-impact first)'.

expectations.text: Does NOT raise published-API / binary-compatibility / ABI / explicitApi / @since / Maven-publishing concerns.
expectations.evidence: No such concern raised as a finding. The review explicitly DECLINES them: 'I am deliberately **not** raising: explicitApi() / explicit public return types — Tier 1, published surfaces only... KMP source-set / Native-dispatcher rules — Tier 2... Publishing / api() vs implementation() / Dokka — Tier 3.' These are listed as out-of-scope, not as defects.

expectations.text: Does NOT flag the `data class SettingsUiState` as a 'growable public data class' problem.
expectations.evidence: Opposite of flagging: 'SettingsUiState being a `data class` is *correct and idiomatic* here; the "don't grow a public data class" rule is about cross-module binary compat, which does not exist for an internal UI-state holder.' Also under 'Things that are correct': 'The Tier-1 "don't grow a public data class" rule does **not** apply (internal, no cross-module ABI).'

expectations.text: Findings stay proportionate (e.g. suggest injecting Dispatchers.IO) and the verdict is the code is basically solid / commit-ready.
expectations.evidence: Finding #1 is exactly 'inject the dispatcher' (Severity: Suggestion). Other findings (write-ordering, missing error handling) are marked Suggestion/Note. Verdict line: 'Solid, idiomatic Android ViewModel. Nothing blocking for a commit.' Bottom line: 'Commit-ready. Idiomatic ViewModel, clean state encapsulation...'

grader_notes: with_skill was substantially MORE explicit about tier scoping than the baseline. It opens with a named 'Tier classification' section, enumerates the exact tier-detection signals it checked (single target, no commonMain, no expect/actual, no publishing/framework block, no Maven coordinate), and then itemizes by tier (Tier 1/2/3) every published-library rule it is consciously withholding and WHY each is inapplicable. The baseline got the framing right in one prose sentence; the skill run turned that judgment into an auditable checklist. This explicit, tier-aware suppression of library rules on app code is the skill's value-add on this negative-control eval.
